\mxunit{enrichment-lattice-paths-solutions}{Paths, combinations and Pascal}
\mxsubtitle{High school · counting \textperiodcentered{} Worked solutions \textperiodcentered{} 05}

\begin{exercise}
Find $C(8,2)$ and explain why it equals $C(8,6)$.
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
$C(8,2) = 8 \times  \frac{7}{2} = 28$. Choosing two excluded objects is equivalent to choosing six included objects.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
Count monotone paths from $(0,0)$ to $(4,3)$.
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
Choose four rightward steps among seven: $C(7,4) = 35$.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
How many of these paths pass through $(2,1)$?
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
$C(3,2) \times  C(4,2) = 3 \times  6 = 18$.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
Choose a team of three from eight people. Two specified people cannot be together. How many teams remain possible?
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
There are $C(8,3) = 56$ teams. Exactly 6 contain both specified people. Therefore 50 teams remain.
\end{solution}

\begin{problem}[Investigate, justify, conclude]
Count monotone paths from $(0,0)$ to $(5,4)$ that avoid $A(2,1)$ and $B(3,3)$. Count all paths, then those passing through A, through B and through both. Explain why the last category must be added back.
\end{problem}
\begin{solution}
Total: $C(9,5) = 126$. Through A: $C(3,2)C(6,3) = 60$. Through B: $C(6,3)C(3,2) = 60$. Through both: $3 \times  C(3,1) \times  3 = 27$. Paths through both were subtracted twice; adding them back once gives $126 - 60 - 60 + 27 = 33$.
\end{solution}
